# Download + load + run in 3 lines

from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForCausalLM

import torch

# Load separately for fine-tuning, batching, or custom logic
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3.5-27B")

                "Qwen/Qwen3.5-27B", device_map="auto"

SAM3: Text-Only Prompt



New in SAM 3: Promptable Concept Segmentation. You can now segment by name!
Hugging Face Docs | Ultralytics Docs






Gated Model: SAM 3 requires users to accept the license on Hugging Face before downloading. Ensure you are logged in using huggingface-cli login.



from transformers import Sam3Model, Sam3Processor
from PIL import Image
import torch

model     = Sam3Model.from_pretrained("facebook/sam3")
processor = Sam3Processor.from_pretrained("facebook/sam3")

image = Image.open("highway.jpg").convert("RGB")

# Segment by concept name
inputs = processor(images=image, text="yellow school bus", return_tensors="pt")

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)

# Post-process to get binary masks and confidence scores
results = processor.post_process_instance_segmentation(
    outputs, 
    threshold=0.5,
    target_sizes=inputs.get("original_sizes").tolist()
)[0]

print(f"Detected {len(results['masks'])} buses")

title: HuggingFace for Computer Vision
text:
SAM3: Negative Box Refinement



SAM3 uses Concepts (text or templates). If a text prompt is too broad, use negative boxes to exclude specific areas.



# Segment "handle" but exclude the oven handle using a negative box
text = "handle"
# Box in [x1, y1, x2, y2] format
oven_handle_box = [40, 183, 318, 204]

inputs = processor(
    images=image, 
    text=text, 
    input_boxes=[[oven_handle_box]], 
    input_boxes_labels=[[0]], # 0 = negative (exclude this region)
    return_tensors="pt"
).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)

results = processor.post_process_instance_segmentation(
    outputs, threshold=0.5, target_sizes=inputs.get("original_sizes").tolist()
)[0]



Label conventions: 1 = Positive (include), 0 = Negative (exclude).

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
From Part 1: f(image) → output

In Part 1: a model is f, learned from data, mapping image → output.

That’s what it does — not how it learns.


This section: how f goes from random guesses to useful predictions.





We’ll build it up from a toy color classifier, then scale to YOLO.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
The Learning Loop

Training isn’t magic; it’s a repetitive cycle of refinement.


Define a Function: Create a mapping from data to predictions (\(f\)).




Evaluate Performance: Measure exactly how “wrong” the current function is (Loss).




Optimize & Repeat: Update the function’s parameters to reduce that error (Optimization).






We start with a guess and “tune” the knobs until we’re happy with the results.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
A Naive Classifier from Color
Task: Is this a red car? — output should eventually be a probability.

Simplest feature: average red pixel value (0-255).
\[f(\text{image}) \approx x_{\text{red}}(\text{image})\]

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
section: From a Number to a Probability
text:
From a Number to a Probability

The average red value lands in [0, 255] — but it’s just a raw number. To learn, we need parameters.

Add weights to calculate a score (\(z\)):
\[z = w \cdot x_{\text{red}} + b\]



\(w\) (Weight): How much does “redness” matter?
\(b\) (Bias): Baseline assumption (are red cars common?)



Now \(z\) depends on \(w\) and \(b\) — but it’s unbounded: it can go negative or exceed 1.





Problem: We need a function that maps any real number → [0, 1] for a probability.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
The Sigmoid


The Squashing Function
\[\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]


Large +z → near 1.0
Large −z → near 0.0
z = 0 → 0.5














Prediction: \[f(\text{image}) = \sigma(\underbrace{w \cdot x_{\text{red}} + b}_{\text{score } z})\]

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
section: Why Metrics Aren’t Enough for Learning
text:
Why Metrics Aren’t Enough for Learning
We have predictions. From Part 3, we know how to grade them — mAP, Precision, Recall. So why not just train against those?





Discrete (Problem)


mAP, Precision, Recall
Small weight changes → zero change in the metric.









Smooth (Solution)


Training Loss
Every tiny adjustment is mathematically measurable.
















So we need a smooth substitute. Enter the loss.






We skip deeper technical details to keep the intuition front and center.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Measuring Wrongness — The Idea

To evaluate our model, we need a mathematical definition of “wrongness.”






🤔 Instinct


Measure the raw difference between target and prediction.

\(\text{err} = y - f(x)\)












🚨 The Flaw


Target = \(0\), Prediction = \(1\)

\(0 - 1 = \mathbf{-1}\)

The model seeks the lowest number. It thinks \(-1\) is better than \(0\) (perfect)!











💡 The Fix


A mistake of \(-1\) is just as bad as \(+1\).
Square the difference:

\(\text{err}^2 = (y - f(x))^2\)

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Measuring Wrongness — Example
Let’s start with a random guess: w = 0.06, b = -14.0



Image A — Red Car

\(x_{\text{red}} \approx 247\)






Image B — Not a Red Car

\(x_{\text{red}} \approx 212\)


















Score: \(z = 0.06(247) - 14.0 = 0.82\)
Prediction: \(f(x) = \sigma(0.82) \approx 0.69\)
\(\text{err} = (1 - 0.69)^2 = \mathbf{0.10}\)











Score: \(z = 0.06(212) - 14.0 = -1.28\)
Prediction: \(f(x) = \sigma(-1.28) \approx 0.22\)
\(\text{err} = (0 - 0.22)^2 = \mathbf{0.05}\)

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Formalizing the Loss (MSE)

To get a single metric for the whole dataset, we average these squared errors.

For our two images: Loss = \(\frac{0.10 + 0.05}{2}\) = 0.075


This is called Mean Squared Error (MSE): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(y_i - f(x_i)\bigr)^2\]





Note: We use MSE here for simplicity to build intuition. In practice, modern classifiers use Cross-Entropy Loss, which mathematically penalizes highly-confident wrong guesses much more harshly.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Following the Gradient
Two knobs (w, b). The gradient points where loss drops fastest. Step a little that way. Repeat. → gradient descent.






Learning Rate: The size of the step. Too large = overshoot; too small = takes forever.
Epochs: Repeating this process for the entire dataset.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
section: Scaling Up: From Color to YOLO
text:
Scaling Up: From Color to YOLO
Our toy: 2 weights, 1 feature (avg red).

YOLO — same idea, scaled:

Millions of weights, learns its own features via Convolutions (filters that automatically detect edges/textures/shapes).
Answers many questions per object: where (box), what (class), how sharp (boundary).



One loss isn’t enough → YOLO sums several, one per question.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
YOLO’s Loss: Three Signals
Total loss = sum of three components, each catching a different mistake:




Component
Also called
What it penalizes




Box Loss
box_loss
Wrong coordinates


Class Loss
cls_loss
Wrong label





\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \lambda_{\text{box}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{box}} + \lambda_{\text{cls}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}\]

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Train vs. Validation

To train a robust AI, split your data:

Train Set (~80%): Data the model actively learns from.
Validation Set (~20%): Unseen data evaluated during training to measure performance (mAP).

Crucial: Never train on validation data! This causes Data Leakage where the model memorizes answers but fails in the real world.



Split your data automatically using Ultralytics Data Split or using the Platform.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Data Leakage: The Silent Killer

The Problem: Validation/test data accidentally ends up in the training set.
The Danger: Val metrics look “perfect,” but the model fails in production.
How to Avoid: - Use autosplit() for automatic, safe partitioning. - Avoid manually copying images between split folders. - Check for duplicates/hashes before training.



Suspiciously perfect metrics? Check for leakage!

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Transfer Learning

.pt (Pretrained weights): Starts with general features (edges, shapes) from large datasets. Fast training, needs little data. (Always recommended!)
.yaml (Architecture Definition): Blank blueprint. Random weights, meaning you train entirely from scratch.

Use a .pt model for all custom dataset training to leverage Transfer Learning.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
Important Hyperparameters

epochs (Default: 100): Pass through the ENTIRE dataset. More = learns more, but risks overfitting.
batch (Default: 16): Images processed at once.

Higher = faster, stable, takes more GPU memory.
Smaller = adds noise, longer training.
Pro-tip: Use batch: -1 for AutoBatch to maximize your GPU memory!

imgsz (Default: 640): Target image size. Larger sizes (e.g., 1024) capture more detail but use more RAM.
device (Default: ’’): Specify GPUs (e.g., device=0,1) to trigger multi-GPU training!
Learning Rate (lr0) (Default: 0.01): Controls step size—too large and the ball overshoots, too small and training is slow.
Weight Decay (Default: 0.0005): Penalizes large weights to prevent memorization (🔴 Overfitting).
Patience (patience) (Default: 100): Stop training if validation metrics haven’t improved for \(N\) epochs.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
The Training Spectrum
Every training run lands somewhere on this spectrum — knowing where is the first step to fixing it.








🔴 Overfitting


Model memorizes training data.

Train mAP >> Val mAP
Val loss starts rising

Too much capacity for your data










🟢 Just Right


Model generalizes to new data.

Train ≈ Val, both high
Both losses converge low

The goal — stay here










🟠 Underfitting


Model never learned the patterns.

Both Train and Val mAP low
Losses barely decrease

Too little capacity or training

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 4
text:
🔴 Overfitting: The Symptom

The model memorizes training data instead of learning general patterns.



What you see:

Train loss ↓, Val loss ↑

Models pre-trained on the COCO dataset recognize 80 common classes right out of the box. Using .pt models means we utilize these pre-learned weights without training!

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 1
text:
From probs to top1












Ultralytics pre-computes the answer for us:

probs: Raw probability array for all classes.
probs.top1 → 0 : Index of the highest-probability class.
probs.top1conf → 0.95 : Its confidence score.






Single-Class vs. Multi-Label Classification We just read top1 that is single-class (one winner). But because probs scores every class, we can also do multi-label classification: keep all classes whose probability exceeds a threshold (e.g., prob > 0.50) to assign several labels to one image.

text:
Confidence: Model’s Belief vs. Ground Truth

Question: Does conf=1.0 mean there is a true object 100% of the time?



Answer: No.


Confidence is just a “feeling”: How strongly the model believes this is the answer.
It does NOT guarantee the answer is correct in the real world.


You’ll learn how to actually measure correctness in Part 4 using Precision and Recall

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 1
text:
Mapping to Bounding Boxes












Mapping to \((x_{min}, y_{min}, x_{max}, y_{max})\):
\[
\begin{align*}
x_{min} &= cx - \frac{w}{2} = 7.5 - 4.0 = 3.5 \\
y_{min} &= cy - \frac{h}{2} = 7.5 - 3.5 = 4.0 \\
x_{max} &= cx + \frac{w}{2} = 7.5 + 4.0 = 11.5 \\
y_{max} &= cy + \frac{h}{2} = 7.5 + 3.5 = 11.0
\end{align*}
\]

Rarely does an image contain exactly one object!

YOLO evaluates the image and can predict multiple bounding boxes at once.
The single 6-element array [cx, cy, w, h, conf, cls] is stacked \(N\) times.
Resulting Output Shape: \((N, 6)\) (where \(N\) is the number of detected objects).

Deep Dive: Accessing Bounding Boxes
The result.boxes object provides several ways to access coordinates:

.xyxy: \([x_{min}, y_{min}, x_{max}, y_{max}]\) (Top-left, Bottom-right)
.xywh: \([c_x, c_y, w, h]\) (Center coordinates, width, height)

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 1
text:
The Problem with Absolute Pixels
Why not just train the model on absolute pixel values like w = 8.0?






Images come in all shapes and sizes (4K, 1080p, square, portrait).
A car that is 800 pixels wide in a 4K image might only be 200 pixels wide in a 1080p image.
If the model learns “cars are 800 pixels wide”, it will fail on smaller images!

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 1
text:
The Solution: Normalized Coordinates

Instead of pixels, we teach the model using fractions of the image size (0.0 to 1.0).



\(cx_{norm} = cx_{pixel} / image\_width\)
\(w_{norm} = w_{pixel} / image\_width\)



A car that takes up half the image width is always \(w = 0.5\), regardless of whether the image is 4K or 1080p!



Training vs. Predicting You MUST provide normalized coordinates (0.0 to 1.0) when training the model. However, when you use model.predict(), the Ultralytics Python API conveniently un-normalizes them back into standard absolute pixels (like boxes.xyxy) for immediate use!

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 1
text:
SAHI: Sliced Aided Hyper Inference
Problem: Tiny objects in high-res images (e.g., 4K) often vanish when resized to 640px.


Solution — SAHI:

Slice the large image into small, overlapping tiles.
Run YOLO on each tile at full resolution.
Merge all detections back together automatically.




SAHI is a wrapper around inference — no retraining needed. Use it when objects are small relative to the full frame.

model = YOLO("weights/yolo26n.pt")
# Use track() with stream=True for memory-efficient video processing
results = model.track(source="path/to/video.mp4", stream=True)

# Iterate through the video frames
for result in results:
    boxes = result.boxes
    if boxes.id is not None:
        # Extract IDs as a list of integers
        ids = boxes.id.int().tolist()
        print(f"Tracking IDs: {ids}")  # e.g., [1, 2]

text:
How We See: Light and The Human Eye



1. Illumination: Light from a source (e.g., the sun) hits an object.
2. Reflection: The object absorbs some colors and reflects others.
3. Capture: Reflected light enters the eye through the pupil.
4. Processing: The lens focuses light onto the retina. Photoreceptors (rods and cones) convert it to electrical signals for the brain.

title: Digital Image Foundations
text: How Computers “See”: The Digital Camera

title: Digital Image Foundations
text:
How Computers “See”: Step by Step

1. Capture: Just like the eye, the camera captures reflected light.
2. Lens & Aperture: Light enters through an opening (aperture) and is focused by glass lenses.
3. The Sensor: Instead of a retina, light hits a digital sensor (CMOS/CCD).
4. Digitization: Millions of sensor pixels convert photons into electrical charges, creating a digital matrix (usually 8-bit).







Note: In reality, lenses flip the image upside-down, and color sensors use a Bayer Filter to capture Red, Green, or Blue at each pixel.

text:
Coordinates vs. Array Indexing



We think in geometry: (x, y) = (width, height).
NumPy thinks in matrices: matrix[row, col] = matrix[y, x].
This causes endless confusion when cropping with bounding boxes (x1, y1, x2, y2).

# WRONG (Crops wrong area or crashes)
crop = img[x1:x2, y1:y2] 

# CORRECT (y = row, x = col)
crop = img[y1:y2, x1:x2]

title: Real World Video Engineering
text:
The Standard Loop
A standard OpenCV inference loop looks like this:
import cv2
from ultralytics import YOLO

cap = cv2.VideoCapture(0)
model = YOLO('yolov8n.pt')

while True:
    ret, frame = cap.read()       # Block 1
    if not ret: break
    
    results = model(frame)        # Block 2
    annotated = results[0].plot() # Block 3
    
    cv2.imshow("Camera", annotated)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) == ord('q'): break

title: Real World Video Engineering
text:
Where Time Goes
In a synchronous while loop, every operation waits for the previous one to finish.

cap.read(): ~30ms (Waiting for the camera sensor or network packet)
model(frame): ~20ms (Inference on GPU)
cv2.imshow(): ~5ms (Rendering)

Total Time per Frame: ~55ms (Max ~18 FPS)
If you are reading an RTSP stream (e.g. from an IP Camera) that sends 30 FPS, reading frames slower than they arrive causes a buffer overflow resulting in massive delay (lag).

title: Real World Video Engineering
text:
Multithreading in Python
To prevent the model inference from slowing down the camera reading, we can put them on separate Threads.

Thread 1 (Producer): Constantly reads frames from the camera as fast as possible.
Thread 2 (Consumer): Takes the latest frame and runs YOLO inference on it.

title: Real World Video Engineering
text:
The Producer-Consumer Pattern
We need a safe way for Thread 1 to hand the frame to Thread 2. We use a Thread-Safe Queue (queue.Queue).
from queue import Queue
from threading import Thread

# A queue to hold our frames
frame_queue = Queue(maxsize=1) 
Why maxsize=1? For real-time applications (like security cameras), we only care about the most recent frame. If inference is slow, we want to drop old frames, not process a backlog of delayed footage.

title: Real World Video Engineering
text:
The Async Reader Class
import cv2
from threading import Thread
from queue import Queue

class AsyncCamera:
    def __init__(self, src=0):
        self.cap = cv2.VideoCapture(src)
        self.q = Queue(maxsize=1)
        self.running = True
        # Start the background thread
        Thread(target=self._reader, daemon=True).start()

    def _reader(self):
        while self.running:
            ret, frame = self.cap.read()
            if not ret: break
            
            # Clear queue if full (drop old frame)
            if self.q.full():
                try: self.q.get_nowait()
                except: pass
                
            # Put new frame in queue
            self.q.put(frame)

title: Real World Video Engineering
text:
Consuming the Queue
Now our main loop only asks the Queue for frames, never blocking on the camera!
camera = AsyncCamera(0)
model = YOLO('yolov8n.pt')

while True:
    # Get the latest frame from the background thread
    frame = camera.q.get() 
    
    # Run inference
    results = model(frame)
    annotated = results[0].plot()
    
    cv2.imshow("Async Cam", annotated)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) == ord('q'): 
        break
        
camera.running = False

title: Real World Video Engineering
text:
Summary

Synchronous loops (cap.read() + inference()) cause lag on live streams.
Producer-Consumer Pattern: Separating reading and processing solves this.
queue.Queue (maxsize=1): The safest way to pass frames between threads and enforce dropping old frames to maintain real-time performance.

Scenario: Smart Parking Camera

A camera at a parking entrance classifies each frame as Car Present or Not:


Dataset: 24 hours, 10,000 frames (~9s interval)




Count

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
The Problem with Accuracy
A “lazy” model that always predicts “Empty”:


Finds 0 cars
Gets all 9,500 empty spots correct



\[Accuracy = \frac{9{,}500}{10{,}000} = 95\%\]


95% Accuracy — yet it never detects a single car. This is the Class Imbalance Problem.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Balanced Accuracy: A Quick Fix
Instead of overall accuracy, we average the per-class accuracies so each class counts equally.

Applied to our “Lazy” Model:

Car Accuracy: 0 / 500 = 0%
Empty Accuracy: 9,500 / 9,500 = 100%
Balanced Accuracy: \((0\% + 100\%) / 2 = \mathbf{50\%}\)



Balanced Accuracy correctly flags the lazy model as a failure, even though its “standard” accuracy was 95%!

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Balanced Accuracy: The Hidden Problem
What if our model catches every car, but is “trigger-happy”?















Car Accuracy: 100%
Empty Accuracy: 80%

\[\frac{100\% + 80\%}{2} = \mathbf{90\%}\]





90% looks great — but that’s 1,900 false alarms hidden inside the score.








The TN “Trap”: The 7,600 True Negatives (correctly ignoring empty spots) are what inflate the accuracy while the false alarms flood your system.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Precision and Recall
Two metrics that ignore True Negatives entirely (correctly classified Empty spot):

Precision: When the model flags a “Car”, is it actually a Car? (Quality) \[Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\]
Recall: Out of all actual Cars, how many did the model find? (Quantity) \[Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\]

Raising or lowering your confidence threshold shifts the balance:


🎯 High Threshold (0.80)

↓ Recall (more misses)

A 0 in either metric drags the whole score down — you can’t hide behind one strong number.

Case Study: Translating Metrics to ROI
Accuracy and F1 are great for engineers, but management speaks one language: Money.

Scenario: A Digital Factory produces high-end circuit boards. We deploy a YOLO model to detect “Defective Solders” before shipping.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Cost of Every Prediction
Every prediction in our Digital Factory has a tangible financial consequence:

✅ True Positive (TP): Defect caught, scrapped early. (Baseline)
✅ True Negative (TN): Good board ships. (Baseline)
❌ False Negative (FN): Defective board ships to a customer. Cost: $500 (Warranty, shipping, brand damage).
⚠️ False Positive (FP): Good board flagged as defective. Requires manual inspection. Cost: $25 (Labor).

Predicted: Good

Cost: $0

Cost: $500 each


Actual: Good

Baselines: The Cost of “Dumb” Decisions
What if we didn’t use AI at all? Let’s look at the financial impact of the two simplest “Dummy” strategies:

Assume every board is Good

False Negatives (FN): 500

⚙️ “Scrap Everything”

The Conclusion: Even a “basic” model saves the company hundreds of thousands of dollars per batch. Now let’s see how much more we can save by optimizing.

Optimizing for Profit, Not Just F1
Remember how F1 balances Precision and Recall? When money is involved, the balance changes.


Option A: Max F1 Score
Balanced threshold (conf=0.35)

FN (Missed): 76 boards \(\times \$500\) = \(\$38,000\)
FP (False Alarms): 0 boards \(\times \$25\) = \(\$0\)

FP (False Alarms): 4 boards \(\times \$25\) = \(\$100\)
Total Loss: $6,600






By lowering our threshold and accepting a few False Positives, we saved the business over $31,400 per batch. We optimized for the business metric, not the machine learning metric.

The Threshold Dilemma
All metrics so far (\(F1\), \(ROI\), \(Precision\)) require us to choose a threshold first.


🎯 The “Decision” View
Useful for deployment. “At 0.45 confidence, what is my profit?”

Pick one point on the curve.
Optimize for a specific business case.
Good for operational decisions.


📊 The “Model” View
Useful for benchmarking. “Is this model fundamentally better than the last one?”

Evaluate over all thresholds.
Compare architectures fairly.
This is where Average Precision (AP) comes in.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
The PR Curve & Average Precision (AP)




Step 1: Gather We take every “Car” prediction the model made across the whole test set.



Step 2: Sort We sort them from highest confidence (e.g., \(0.99\)) to lowest (e.g., \(0.10\)).



Step 3: Calculate We calculate Precision and Recall at every single step of that sorted list.



















Average Precision (AP) is simply the area under this Precision-Recall (PR) curve!

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
section: From Binary to Multi-Class: One-vs-Rest (most common)
text:
From Binary to Multi-Class: One-vs-Rest (most common)
When we have many classes, we reduce the problem to binary by isolating each class.


Pick one class as Positive — everything else is Negative. Repeat for every class.




This logic applies to any binary metric like Precision, Recall, AP, etc.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Per-Class Recall Formula
For a specific class \(i\), treat it as “positive” and all others as “negative”:
\[Recall_i = \frac{TP_i}{TP_i + FN_i}\]






\(TP_i\) — instances of class \(i\) correctly predicted as class \(i\)







\(FN_i\) — instances of class \(i\) predicted as any other class

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Ways to Aggregate Per-Class Scores
Once you have a score per class, you combine them into a single number:









Strategy
Formula
Character




Macro
\(\frac{\sum M_i}{n}\)
All classes equally weighted


Micro
\(\frac{\sum \text{Num}_i}{\sum \text{Denom}_i}\)
Pooled counts (treats every sample equally)


Weighted
\(\frac{\sum M_i \cdot S_i}{\sum S_i}\)
Weighted by class size (Support)





\(M_i\): Metric per class (\(P, R, AP\))  \(S_i\): Support (class size)  \(\text{Num}_i / \text{Denom}_i\): Numerator / Denominator (e.g., \(TP / (TP+FP)\))






mAP = Macro-Average of per-class AP scores. Every class contributes equally.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
But Does Location Matter?
Precision and Recall measure whether a classification is correct.
For object detection, the model must also get the location right.


A confident prediction placed in the wrong spot is still a wrong prediction.



That’s where Intersection over Union (IoU) comes in.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Intersection over Union (IoU)
How perfectly does the predicted bounding box overlap the ground truth box?









Rule of Thumb: A prediction is typically considered a “True Positive” (correct) if the IoU is > 0.50.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
The “Double Penalty” of IoU
A prediction must be accurate in location (\(IoU \ge 0.5\)) to count as a True Positive (TP).












What happens when \(IoU < 0.5\)?



It hurts your score twice:

FP: The bad box is a false alarm
FN: The real object is counted as missed




One poor prediction = penalised as both an extra detection and a missed object.

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Handling Multiple Detections
A common question is: “What if the model predicts multiple boxes for the exact same object?”












Rule: One Ground Truth = Only One TP

The Winner: Highest IoU (Pred 1) becomes the True Positive (TP).
The Duplicate: Extra boxes (Pred 2) become False Positives (FP).

title: Ultralytics YOLO Foundations: Part 3
text:
Mean Average Precision (mAP)

mAP50: Accuracy considering only “easy” detections (IoU > 0.50).
mAP50-95: The strict evaluation averaged across multiple IoU thresholds (from 0.50 to 0.95).

Edge & Mobile Deployment
Ultralytics supports a wide range of hardware-specific formats.

NVIDIA Jetson: TensorRT (.engine)
Apple (iPhone/Mac): CoreML (.mlpackage)
Android / IoT: TFLite (.tflite)
Web Browsers: TensorFlow.js / ONNX.js
Vision Sensors: Sony IMX500 (Raspberry Pi AI Camera).


Pro Tip: Use the half=True or int8=True argument when exporting for mobile to keep the app size small!

Production Best Practices
To ensure a smooth transition from development to the real world:

Warm-up: Run 1-2 dummy inferences to initialize hardware/drivers before processing live data.
Environment Parity: Match your production OS/Drivers to your testing environment (use Docker!).
Input Validation: Ensure production images are the same resolution as training (e.g., imgsz=640).
Monitoring: Log inference times and confidence scores to detect Data Drift.
